title: book review: biocatalysis and enzyme technology
display_name: Book review: Biocatalysis and Enzyme Technology
abstract: biocatalysis and enzyme technology the second edition of this text book by klaus buchholz, volker kasche and uwe theo bornscheuer is updated to provide the latest information in biocatalysis and enzyme technology. book review by mikhail rabinovich. biocatalysts and enzyme technology by klaus buchholz, volker kasche and uwe theo bornscheuer, wiley, 2012, 626 pages. isbn 978-3-527-32989-2 prof. mikhail l. rabinovich ph.d., d.sc. mirabi@mail.ru*, * a.n.bach institute of biochemistry, russian academy of sciences, moscow, russia long ago, as a student in the faculty chaired by the nobel laureate nikolay semenov at moscow university, i listened to the brilliant lectures on biocatalysis of professors ilya berezin and karel martinek. at that time, the students learned the first available 3d structures of lysozyme and carboxypeptidase a, published in the 1960s by the groups of d. c. phillips and w. n. lipscomb; the mechanism of -chymotrypsin acylation-deacylation from the publications of m. l. bender's group; and the king-altman method to obtain kinetic equations for complex enzyme reactions. apart from the fundamental monograph of m. dixon and e. c. webb, the freshly issued lecture course of w. p. jencks catalysis in chemistry and enzymology was the most popular textbook. the available literature on enzyme engineering was in contrast sparse. since the 1970s, applied biocatalysis experienced a burst of development following the pioneering studies of e. katchalski-katzir, k. mosbach, and i. chibata, many of which were published in the first dedicated journal to the topic, biotechnology and bioengineering and greatly inspired the enzyme engineers. this resulted in an exponential growth in our knowledge of biocatalysis and enzyme engineering. biotechnology journal has recently also devoted a special issue to the tremendous progress in biocatalysis [1]. the authors of the new textbook on biocatalysis, biocatalysis and enzyme technology, well known for their extensive research contributions in the field, and also from the first edition of this textbook, have therefore set themselves a challenging task. because of a finite volume of any textbook, authors must always have a sixth sense of a proper balance between basic knowledge, which can be delivered in various levels of depth, and its numerous applications, which can be infinitely updated. some authors also try to create a textbook based mostly on their own studies, which do not necessarily provide the best teaching material. the authors of this textbook seem to have safely escaped being between scylla and charybdis and created a well-balanced course material for training of practical specialists in enzyme engineering. the first two chapters introduce the historical perspective of the utilization of enzymes as highly selective, effective, and environmentally friendly catalysts. a basic knowledge on the enzyme structure, catalytic mechanisms, kinetically significant intermediates, transition states, regio- and enantioselectivity, inhibition with products and excess of substrate is considered. along with protein stability, effects of ph, ionic strength, and temperature, the concept of kinetically and thermodynamically controlled enzymatic reactions is described and illustrated. the subsequent chapters consecutively introduce the basic principles of selection and engineering of an appropriate biocatalyst, its industrial production, purification and recovery, and a number of large-scale applications. a relatively short but comprehensive and very well updated chapter 3 (enzyme discovery and protein engineering) highlights the importance of adequate high-throughput screening assays in rational and computational design of the tailored biocatalysts with greater selectivity, higher catalytic activity and stability, optimal ph and temperature profiles, and lower product inhibition. a wide variety of stereospecific organic reactions carried out with biocatalysts is reviewed in chapter 4 and the concept of dynamic kinetic resolution is introduced. the problem of cofactor regeneration is also concisely stated. among the many advantages of the textbook is an introduction to the novel techniques in selecting an appropriate biocatalyst including metagenomics as well as metabolic engineering of whole cells as biocatalysts for multistep transformations (chapter 5). problems arising from the production and recovery of heterologously expressed enzymes, such as wrong folding resulting in inclusion bodies accumulation, the need of secretion and glycosylation, accumulation in periplasm of a host cell, and possible solutions of these problems including renaturation are discussed in chapter 6 (enzyme production and purification). along with basic principles of chromatographic purification, continuous chromatography with a simulated moving bed, multicolumn countercurrent solvent gradient purification (mcsgh), new mixed mode (ion exchange/hydrophobic) absorbents, and reduction of the chromatography steps by membrane technology, are also addressed in this chapter. another distinguishing feature of this textbook is the section on the national and international regulations covering the use of enzymes from both wild-type and recombinant organisms. this important issue is often ignored by other textbooks. chapter 7 is focused on the application of soluble native and recombinant enzymes in starch processing and biofuel production. a separate section is devoted to the recovery of soluble enzymes or retention of catalytically active cells after biocatalytic transformation of a substrate using various types of ultra- and microfiltration modules. it is a pity that this chapter does not include the peculiarities of enzymatic reactions with polymeric (often insoluble) substrates, for which the meaning of a substrate concentration differs from that of monomeric soluble substrates and the apparent kinetic constants that gradually change during the course of a reaction. worth noting, most of the listed large-scale applications of soluble enzymes (proteases, cellulases, amylases, xylanases) belong to this type of enzymatic reactions, where the equations of box 7.1, particularly their integrated forms, need to be applied with caution, if at all. this omission is however partially corrected in section 12.2.2.4 of chapter 12 (case studies), where some remarks on the limited applicability of simple kinetic models to the enzymatic hydrolysis of cellulose are made. ... a distinguishing feature is the section on the national and international regulations covering the use of enzymes from both wild-type and recombinant organisms... covalent and noncovalent procedures for immobilization of isolated enzymes or enzymes within dead cells, and immobilization of living microorganisms or whole cells are described in chapters 8 and 9, respectively. application of immobilized enzymes is illustrated in chapter 8 with the examples of glucose isomerisation, production of antibiotics, and re-esterification of lipids. application of magnetic particles for immobilization is briefly mentioned in chapter 11. yet another out of many advantages of this textbook is the inclusion of both theoretical and practical exercises, as well as exercises that require the use of corresponding databases. some exercises leave a space for speculations to stimulate the creative thinking of the students. chapter 9 includes both self-immobilization of microorganisms and their artificial immobilization by adsorption, entrapment in soft gels, covalent binding, microencapsulation, or cross-linking. mass transfer of oxygen and nutrient supply to the immobilized microorganisms as well as product diffusion out of the catalyst particles are also briefly considered. chapter 9 also concisely addresses mammalian cells immobilization on microcarriers to produce glycosylated human recombinant proteins. the focus of this chapter is, however, anaerobic wastewater treatment, denitrification, and deodorization of toxic and malodorous gases with immobilized microorganisms in the fluidized bed, trickle bed reactors, and biofilters. as an important update of the first edition, the section microbial fuel cells was included that describes the recent success in the utilization of geobacter and some other biofilm-forming anaerobic bacteria on porous conductive surfaces for the direct transfer of electrons from oxidized organic wastewater pollutants to the electric circuit. worthy of noting is the practical exercises to this chapter such as training in the immobilization of yeast or microbial cultures for ethanol fermentation or wastewater treatment. an advantage is the inclusion of both theoretical and practical exercises... some exercises leave space for speculations to stimulate the creative thinking of the students. chapter 10 introduces the general concepts and definitions of heterogeneous enzyme catalysis and macrokinetics that influence the biocatalyst productivity (space-time yield). the authors provide a moderate level of theoretical depth with a large number of experimental details obtained mostly from their own studies on immobilized penicillin amidase. the principles of calculation of a steady state distribution of substrate and product concentration profiles within the particles of a heterogeneous catalyst are provided and possible reasons of discrepancies between theoretical predictions and experimental data outlined. last but not least, some practical tips and tricks to determine the key characteristics of immobilized biocatalysts and to increase their performance are also provided. enzymatic reactions in the open systems are further considered and performance of the batch and continuous stirred tank reactor (cstr) vs. plug flow reactor compared. this topic is further extended in chapter 11, which also addresses bioreactor design, reaction engineering, process integration, control, and sustainability as well as some environmental issues. chapter 12 (case studies) describes in more detail starch processing, glucose isomerization, production of the 1st- and the 2nd-generation biofuels from biomass, etc. in principle, section 12.2.2 (lignocellulose-based biofuels) could be updated. figure 12.7, for example, illustrates the mechanism of enzymatic hydrolysis of cellulose formulated by the end of 1990s (cf. [2]), whereas currently the role of nonhydrolytic factors (swollenins and the oxidoreductases, namely cel61 and cellobiose dehydrogenase) come also into play [3]. however, this is not a dramatic omission and can be updated by a lecturer if necessary. a very helpful appendix a the world of biotechnology information provides a suitable guide to searching the respective internet resources and warns about the danger of plagiarism and copyright violation for the fans of copy/paste. exercises suppose basic knowledge of protein chemistry and biochemistry as well as experimental skills (chapters 8 and 9). the solutions to the theoretical exercises of all twelve chapters are given in the appendix b. taken together, the authors have successfully fulfilled their task by preparing a versatile introductory course to modern enzyme engineering. they focus on large-scale biocatalytic applications and practical training of future enzyme engineers, leaving aside analytical and electrochemical applications of biocatalysts because of space limitations. the second edition is a comprehensive update of the first edition. for this reason i have taken the liberty for some proposals for the future editions of this remarkable textbook. it seems reasonable to teach the students not only to safely surf in the infinite ocean of biotechnology information, but also to interactively learn a variety of available software for molecular graphics, docking of substrates and inhibitors (e.g. mgl.scripps.edu), simulation and modeling of complex enzymatic reactions, metabolic flows, macrokinetics, reactions in open systems, bioreactor and bioprocess design (e.g. en.bio-soft.net/bioengi.html). many examples of kinetic simulation software, both simple (enzo) and professional (simfit, kintecus, chemkin) are freely available on the internet for educational purposes. by using this software, we don't need to deliver ready formulas for integral kinetics, which would not adequately work for, e. g. polymeric or insoluble substrates. our primary task is to teach our students to understand and express reversible and quasi-irreversible elementary stages of enzymatic reactions, the ranges of corresponding kinetic/equilibrium constants, distinguish between kinetically significant intermediates and transition states, correctly evaluate the effects of temperature on mass transfer, equilibrium, kinetic, and inactivation constants of a free or immobilized biocatalyst. interactively using corresponding numerical methods, one can easily demonstrate, e. g. inactivation of the enzyme in the course of reaction or steady-state multiplicity of enzymatic processes in real systems, and select appropriate optimal regimes. in contrast, some ready formulas such as that placed onto the cover can in fact mislead, since ki,app may differ for the free enzyme and the es complex and depend on the [s]/km ratio. unfortunately, some misprints were also missed in this edition, including rather curious one such as enzymatic hydrolysis of penicillin g at 310 oc (figs. 10.14 and 10.16). other misprints were missed in the formulas 2.8, 2.29, 2.39, and 7.1. in the caption to the fig. 1.9 obviously -galactosidase rather than -glucosidase should be mentioned as an enzyme hydrolyzing lactose. in conclusion, in spite of these remarks addressed mostly to the future editions, it was a real pleasure to carefully study this textbook step by step and i would in any event recommend it worldwide as a basic introductory course in enzyme engineering. mikhail l. rabinovich, ph.d. in kinetics and catalysis, d.sc. in biochemistry, professor in biotechnology, a.n.bach institute of biochemistry, russian academy of sciences, moscow, russia, e-mail: mirabi@mail.ru about the authors born in 1941, klaus buchholz studied chemistry at the universities of saarbr cken and heidelberg in germany, graduating in 1967. in 1969 he received his phd from the tu munich, germany, after which he worked as a researcher at dechema e.v. in frankfurt am main, germany until 1982. in 1981 he was appointed professor at the tu braunschweig, germany, where he then became department head at the institute for agricultural technology and sugar industry. from 1988 onwards he has headed the institute, and also become professor for technology of carbohydrates at the institute for technical chemistry in 1991. his main research areas include enzymatic processes for the modification and synthesis of saccharides, environmental biotechnology and fluidized bed reactors with immobilized biocatalysts. volker kasche, born in 1939, studied chemistry, mathematics, and physics at the university of uppsala, sweden. after receiving his degree in 1964 he spent a year as a nato research fellow at brandeis university, usa. he received his doctorate from the university of uppsala in 1971, and in 1973 became a professor at the university of bremen, germany, and in 1986 at the tu hamburg-harburg, germany. his research focusses on fundamentals of equilibrium and kinetically controlled reactions catalyzed by free and immobilized biocatalysts, the production and purification of biocatalysts, especially penicillin amidases and serine peptidases, as well as mass transfer in chromatography and enzyme technology. born in 1964, uwe bornscheuer studied chemistry at the university of hanover, germany, where he graduated in 1990. after receiving his phd in 1993 from the institute of technical chemistry at the same university, he spent a postdoctoral year at the university of nagoya, japan. he then joined the institute of technical biochemistry, university of stuttgart, germany, where he finished his habilitation in 1998. he has been professor for biotechnology and enzyme catalysis at the institute of biochemistry, university of greifswald, germany, since 1999. professor bornscheuer's main research interest is the protein engineering of enzymes for applications in the synthesis of optically active compounds and in lipid modification.
